title: Breakfast on the beach (John 21:1–19)
hook: a charcoal fire, fish, and three times, do you love me
carry: thou knowest that I love thee

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas, the doubter who said my Lord and my God. Your line was doubt can kneel too. Day seventy-one. A new week: the fire spreads. And it starts with a very small fire on a beach.

Back in Galilee, back where it all began. Peter doesn't know what to do with himself, so he does what he knows. In the Douay-Rheims: "I go a fishing." Six others go with him. They fish all night and catch nothing. At dawn a man on the shore calls out: children, have you caught anything? No. Throw the net on the right side of the boat. They do, and the net is so full they can't haul it in. The beloved disciple looks at the shore and says it: it is the Lord. And Peter, who can't wait for the boat, throws on his coat and jumps into the sea. Today: breakfast.
screen: `I GO A FISHING.` → `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING.` → `IT IS THE LORD.`

segments.voice: On the beach, Jesus already has a fire going, with fish on it and bread. Come and dine, he says. And here's a detail you'd miss in English. The Greek word for that charcoal fire appears only twice in the whole New Testament: here, and in the high priest's courtyard, where Peter stood warming his hands and denied him three times. Same smell of smoke. After breakfast, Jesus turns to Peter. "Simon son of John, lovest thou me more than these?" Peter says: "Yea, Lord, thou knowest that I love thee." Feed my lambs. He asks a second time. Same answer. Tend my sheep. Then a third time, and John says Peter was grieved, because he asked him the third time. Of course he was. He'd said I don't know him three times. Now he's asked do you love me three times. And he answers from the bottom: "Lord, thou knowest all things: thou knowest that I love thee." Jesus doesn't make him grovel. He never mentions the courtyard at all. Each answer comes back with a job: feed my sheep. And at the end, by the same lake where he first called Peter after another night of empty nets, two words: follow me. Catholics read this as Jesus giving Peter the care of his whole flock, part of why they see Peter, and the popes after him, as shepherd of the Church. But look at how the job was given. Not to the one who never failed. To the one who failed, and was loved back, one question at a time.
screen: `A CHARCOAL FIRE, TWICE.` · `DO YOU LOVE ME? THREE TIMES.` · `EACH ANSWER GETS A JOB.` · `FOLLOW ME, AGAIN.` · then, large: `THOU KNOWEST THAT I LOVE THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: undo one failure with one kindness. Settle and breathe. Bring back a time you let someone down, the way Peter did in the courtyard. It doesn't have to be big. Now, instead of replaying it, think of one kind thing you could do for that person, or for someone like them, this week. Not an apology tour. Just one act that points the other way. If you pray, you can answer the question for yourself: do you love me? The bell holds the time.
Breakfast on the beach. A charcoal fire, a full net, and three questions for the man who had said no three times. Today's word.
Your line: thou knowest that I love thee. Today, do the one kindness. Let it answer the old failure for you. Day seventy-one.

howItsDone: Catholics hear this Gospel in the Easter season and read it, with Matthew 16, as part of Peter's commission to shepherd the Church, a role they see continued in the pope.

what it means: the one who denied him three times is asked three times, do you love me, and each answer comes back with a job.
what a scholar hears: anthrakia, a charcoal fire, only here and in the courtyard of the denials. and Catholics read feed my sheep with Matthew 16 as Peter's commission.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of John 21:3, 15, 17 given from memory; confirm (DR may read 'Simon son of John' — confirm the form of the name).
ἀνθρακιά occurs only in John 18:18 and 21:9 in the New Testament. Confirm.
Scholars debate whether the shift between agapao and phileo in 21:15–17 matters; the script leaves it out.
Catholic reading of 21:15–17 as Peter's pastoral commission (CCC 553, 881). Confirm phrasing.

The teach links 'follow me' (John 21:19) back to day 34 (Luke 5:1–11, the first call after a night of empty nets). Luke 5 has no 'follow me' spoken; the earlier wording 'the same two words as on the first day' was changed so it does not claim Jesus said them then. Confirm.
